Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, the expressions (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) always produce the same result. In floating-point arithmetic, however, each intermediate result is usually rounded to the nearest representable value. Changing the order of addition changes the intermediate values, so it can also change where rounding occurs and which information is lost.

For example, suppose a is very large while b and c are much smaller. Adding b to a may produce exactly a in floating-point arithmetic because b is too small to affect the stored significand. If c nearly cancels a, evaluating (a + b) + c can therefore lose b completely. Evaluating a + (b + c) may preserve some or all of b because b first combines with a value of comparable scale. The two mathematically equivalent expressions can consequently differ by several representable steps, and severe cancellation can make their relative difference much larger.

Large matrix multiplications contain many dot products, each of which reduces a sequence of products to a sum. High-performance implementations do not necessarily add these products from left to right. They divide matrices into blocks, distribute work across processor cores or accelerators, use vector instructions, and combine partial sums through reduction trees. Different thread counts, block sizes, scheduling decisions, hardware architectures, or library algorithms can create different reduction orders. Since addition is not associative, these orders can produce slightly different entries in the output matrix.

Fused multiply-add instructions add another source of variation. They compute a product and an addition with a single final rounding, whereas separate multiplication and addition usually involve two roundings. Fused operations are generally more accurate, but their results need not be bit-for-bit identical to results produced without fusion. Some hardware may also use different intermediate precision or handle exceptional values differently.

The discrepancies are often tiny, typically on the scale predicted by floating-point error analysis, but they can accumulate across long dot products. They may become more visible for ill-conditioned data, terms with widely varying magnitudes, or sums involving substantial cancellation. Subsequent nonlinear or threshold-based computations can amplify small differences.

Therefore, mathematically identical matrix multiplications may not be bitwise reproducible when their reduction orders differ. Reproducibility requires controlling the algorithm, thread scheduling, instruction selection, and numerical environment, or using deterministic and sometimes more expensive summation methods. Ordinary tolerance-based comparisons are usually more appropriate than demanding exact equality.
